I disagree. I've found that many of the articles on Wikipedia are very accurate and well sourced.

Let's try putting this another way: Regardless of each article's individual level of accuracy and quality, the content on Wikipedia should not be trusted; follow the citations and decide if the content on the other side of them is trustworthy. The articles can never be better than the sources they cite, and when the sources aren't up to a decent standard of reliability (e.g. because media's reporting on itself, etc.) then the article, no matter how polished and sourced it is, they're still turds.

Don't get me wrong; there's lots of good and correct content on Wikipedia. But that's beside the point. Don't trust; just verify and verify.

What MSP horror stories have you encountered?

Dangerous situations, livid customers, support issues, weird interactions?

Once we had the business owner of one of our clients call saying that someone walked in off the street, told the receptionist he was with tech support and then got on her computer.

The owner saw the receptionist not at her station and investigated. When the owner asked the guy on the computer which company he was with, the guy left in a hurry.

Thankfully we had the system relatively locked down. That office also uses practice management software which is encrypted outside of the workstations - so even if they have AD access on the machine, unless they have credentials to the software they can't do much.

We now use that as an example to scare customers into doing the right thing - strong passwords, encryption on laptops & USB drives, lockout periods. We also started wearing uniform shirts after the incident.
